matching.reasoningTemplate: Progressive exertional dyspnoea with fine bibasal crackles and no fever points to interstitial lung disease.

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e, Ch.304 Interstitial Lung Disease (book pp.2259-2266) and Ch.299 Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis (book pp.2228-2231); supporting material from Ch.295-297 (pp.2199-2213)
clinicalPearls: Diffuse parenchymal lung disease covers >200 heterogeneous conditions; the interstitial space between epithelium and endothelium is the dominant site, but alveolar epithelium and endothelial (airway and vessel) cells also drive pathogenesis (p.2259).

No single piece of data is diagnostic on its own; a confident ILD diagnosis requires the combined weight of clinical, laboratory, PFT, imaging and (when obtained) histopathologic findings, ideally reviewed in a multidisciplinary conference of pulmonologists, rheumatologists, radiologists and pathologists (pp.2259-2260).
Fine end-inspiratory bibasal crackles described as sounding like Velcro being pulled apart are characteristic of fibrotic ILD such as IPF and may be one of the earliest signs (pp.2200, 2261).

Egophony, whispered pectoriloquy and bronchial breath sounds suggest alveolar filling (e.g. pneumonia) rather than interstitial fibrosis (IPF); their absence helps distinguish fibrotic crackles from consolidation (p.2200).

Age strongly shifts pretest probability: IPF is most common in patients over 60 and rare under 50, whereas sarcoidosis, CTD-ILD, LAM and pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically present between ages 20 and 40 (p.2260).
On HRCT, apical-predominant interstitial thickening favours NSIP, whereas a basal and subpleural/dependent predominance favours IPF (p.2211).
A dry cough can be the most prominent symptom of IPF; some patients (even with extensive disease) report no dyspnoea at all (p.2261).
HRCT is now standard of care in initial ILD evaluation and can be diagnostic for IPF in the right clinical context, sparing the patient a lung biopsy (p.2262).

BAL findings can point to specific entities: eosinophilia >25% suggests chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, fat globules in macrophages suggest lipoid pneumonia, and serial bloody lavage indicates diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (p.2262).

A close relative with an idiopathic interstitial pneumonia is among the strongest risk factors for IPF; up to ~20% of pulmonary fibrosis is familial, and diverse IIP subtypes (IPF, NSIP, DIP) can run in the same family (p.2261).
harrison.pathophysiology: ILDs are characterised by remodelling of the interstitium with variable degrees of inflammation and fibrosis, but alveolar epithelial and endothelial cell injury is also central to pathogenesis. The idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (IIPs) are the most common group. In IPF the histologic hallmark is a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern: subpleural reticulation with honeycomb change and fibroblast foci (subepithelial collections of myofibroblasts and collagen) alternating with preserved normal alveolar architecture, producing temporal and spatial heterogeneity. NSIP shows more uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis with honeycombing usually absent and fibroblast foci rare. Genetic studies show that a substantial fraction of familial and even sporadic/idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has a genetic basis: a MUC5B promoter variant (present in ~20% of Caucasians, 35-45% of IPF patients) confers an approximately sixfold risk, and variants in telomere-length genes (TERT, TERC, RTEL1) and surfactant protein genes (SFTPA2) are also implicated. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immune-mediated response to inhaled antigens small enough to reach distal airways and alveoli, driven by dysregulated TH1/TH17 responses with precipitating IgG and innate (Toll-like receptor/MyD88) signalling; chronic HP shares the MUC5B variant with IPF (pp.2259-2266; 2228-2229).
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (UIP pattern; basal/subpleural reticulation, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis) (p.2262)
Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) - cellular or fibrotic; often associated with CTD (p.2263)
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (nonfibrotic or fibrotic; exposure-related granulomatous ILD) (pp.2228, 2304)
Connective tissue disease-associated ILD - systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, polymyositis/dermatomyositis, Sjogren's, SLE (pp.2265-2266)
Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP) - subacute flulike illness, migratory consolidations (p.2264)
Acute interstitial pneumonia (Hamman-Rich syndrome) - acute respiratory distress with diffuse alveolar damage (p.2265)
Smoking-related ILD - respiratory bronchiolitis-ILD (RB-ILD) and desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP) (pp.2263-2264)
Drug-induced ILD - amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, methotrexate, bleomycin, rituximab, anti-TNF agents (p.2261)
Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (young women, diffuse cysts, spontaneous pneumothorax) (p.2260)
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis and pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (p.2304/Fig.304-1)
Granulomatous vasculitides - granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and eosinophilic GPA/Churg-Strauss, which can cause diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (p.2266)
infectionMimics: Pneumocystis pneumonia and other diffuse infections, which should be excluded in the initial diffuse-parenchymal workup (p.2260)
Community-acquired pneumonia - COP is commonly mistaken for pneumonia, and nonfibrotic HP can be misread as a respiratory infection (pp.2229, 2264)
Secondary pulmonary infection in patients with traction bronchiectasis or on immunosuppression, which can produce cough with haemoptysis (p.2261)
Mycobacterial exposure (e.g. Mycobacterium avium complex in hot tub lung) causing HP rather than frank infection (p.2229)
nonInfectiousMimics: Congestive heart failure / hydrostatic pulmonary oedema - basilar crackles and interstitial thickening on imaging overlap with ILD; must be excluded (pp.2211, 2262)
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) - shares diffuse alveolar damage histology with AIP and acute exacerbation of fibrosis (p.2265)
Bronchoalveolar (lepidic) cell carcinoma and lymphangitic carcinomatosis (p.2260)
Organic toxic dust syndrome (OTDS), which mimics HP but needs no prior sensitisation and lacks specific IgG antibodies (p.2230)
additionalInvestigations: Multidisciplinary (MDT) ILD review jointly integrating clinical, radiologic, serologic and pathologic data (pp.2259-2260)
Full PFTs with lung volumes plus DLCO; restriction = reduced TLC with symmetric FEV1/FVC reduction, and a low DLCO may precede volume reduction (less specific, more variable) (pp.2200-2201, 2261)
Serial/repeated FVC measurement - decline correlates with higher mortality and tracks disease progression (p.2261)
CTD/autoantibody serology including anti-CCP, anti-synthetase (e.g. anti-Jo-1, anti-PL-12) antibodies - may reveal an underlying CTD even without other features (pp.2261, 2266)
HRCT chest to define UIP vs NSIP vs COP patterns, extent, honeycombing, and guide biopsy site (p.2262)
Bronchoscopy with BAL - lymphocytosis (with CD4:CD8 <1) characteristic of HP; differential cell counts for eosinophilic pneumonia and DAH (pp.2230, 2262)

Transbronchial biopsy or cryobiopsy; cryobiopsy gives larger yields than forceps but with higher bleeding/pneumothorax risk; VATS surgical biopsy when needed (higher pre-treatment yield, up to ~5% short-term mortality) (pp.2209, 2262)
Serum precipitins / specific IgG for HP - supportive but not sufficient (asymptomatic exposed individuals can be positive; antigen panels often falsely negative) (pp.2229-2230)
Detailed occupational, environmental, avocational, medication and family exposure history (pp.2200, 2261)
Echocardiography to assess for pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain (p.2201)
Genetic evaluation in familial pulmonary fibrosis (MUC5B promoter variant, telomere genes TERT/TERC/RTEL1, surfactant genes) (pp.2261, 2267)
redFlags: Acute exacerbation of IPF - acute (<30 days) onset of respiratory distress and hypoxaemia in a patient with underlying fibrosis, not explained by infection or heart failure; reported mortality >85% (p.2265)
Acute interstitial pneumonia (Hamman-Rich) - acute respiratory distress and hypoxaemia with >50% mortality within 6 months (p.2265)
Haemoptysis suggesting diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (Goodpasture's, GPA) or LAM - warrants urgent evaluation (p.2261)
Honeycombing or extensive fibrosis on HRCT indicating advanced disease and worse prognosis (p.2262)
Signs of advanced disease: cyanosis, digital clubbing and cor pulmonale (p.2262)
Rapidly progressive ILD in anti-Jo-1-positive inflammatory myopathy (p.2266)
A declining FVC on serial testing, which signals elevated mortality risk (p.2261)
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis varies widely by ILD subtype and disease extent. IPF carries a poor prognosis (~50% survival at 3-5 years; pre-antifibrotic-era life expectancy 3-5 years from diagnosis). Idiopathic NSIP is comparatively favourable (>80% 5-year survival), with cellular NSIP doing better than fibrosing NSIP. Reported subtype mortality includes RB-ILD ~25% at 7 years and systemic sclerosis-associated ILD ~20-30% at 10 years; sarcoidosis mortality is generally low but state-dependent. RB-ILD usually has prolonged survival with death from progressive ILD rare. AIP has >50% 6-month mortality with frequent recurrences, though survivors can recover substantial lung function. Acute exacerbations of fibrotic ILD carry very high mortality (>85%). In CTD-ILD, a UIP pattern and more extensive fibrosis (e.g. in RA) predict reduced survival. Chronic fibrotic HP can mirror IPF in radiology and prognosis (pp.2260, 2262-2266; 2229).
pitfalls: Attributing all wheezing to asthma - wheeze can reflect heart failure or other airway narrowing; conversely wheeze is uncommon in ILD but does occur in sarcoidosis, HP and eosinophilic GPA (pp.2200, 2262).
Forgetting that a UIP pattern on biopsy is not unique to IPF - it also occurs in CTD (e.g. RA-associated) ILD (p.2260).
Misreading acute ILD presentations as pneumonia, COPD exacerbation or heart failure, since acute ILD is unusual (p.2260).
Treating presumed IPF with immunosuppression - this has been shown to increase morbidity and mortality in IPF (p.2263).
Relying on PFT pattern to diagnose HP - HP can be restrictive or obstructive, so the pattern is not diagnostic (p.2229).
Over-relying on HP serum precipitin panels - they cover a limited antigen set and frequently give false negatives, and a positive IgG alone does not confirm HP (p.2230).

Confusing HP granulomas with sarcoidosis - HP granulomas are loose/poorly formed and peribronchiolar, whereas sarcoid granulomas are well-formed; caseating granulomas should prompt a search for infection (pp.2230, 2264).
Assuming CTD must be apparent - ILD can precede other CTD features by years or be the sole manifestation (pp.2261, 2265).
Diagnosing IPF without excluding a treatable mimic - heart failure, infection (e.g. PCP) and malignancy must be considered first (p.2260).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison frames ILD pattern recognition rather than a single numeric severity score. ILDs are first split into known cause (occupational e.g. asbestosis/silicosis; drug-induced e.g. amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, methotrexate, bleomycin; systemic/CTD-associated; granulomatous including HP) versus unknown cause (idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, plus rarer entities such as LAM, PAP, PLCH, sarcoidosis). The idiopathic interstitial pneumonias are further classified (per the ATS/ERS consensus) into chronic fibrosing (IPF, idiopathic NSIP), smoking-related (RB-ILD, DIP), and acute/subacute (COP, acute interstitial pneumonia, lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia). The UIP pattern (subpleural, basal reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis) defines IPF, while NSIP shows more ground-glass and rare honeycombing. HP is now classified as nonfibrotic versus fibrotic (replacing the older acute/subacute/chronic terminology). Disease severity is gauged by extent of fibrosis/honeycombing on HRCT, degree of PFT (FVC/DLCO) impairment and its rate of decline, and presence of pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale (pp.2259-2266; 2229).
